evals.prompt: I'm the managing director at Cedar Hollow Playhouse in Asheville, NC — 450-seat house, five-show season, $2.1M budget. We sell one fixed full-season subscription and it's shrinking every year: 2,400 packages three years ago, 1,850 this season. Our renewal rate overall was 62% and our marketing director says we just need to spend more on new-subscriber ads. I want a real plan for the 2027-28 season: what packages to offer, how to price them, and how to stop the bleeding. Can you lay it out?
evals.expected_output: A subscription plan that expands beyond a single fixed package (e.g., fixed full season, mini/CYO, flex pass), prices packages off the single-ticket rate, runs the retain-vs-acquire math to show the new-package target needed to hold flat, sets a cohort renewal pricing ladder and first-year onboarding, and delivers a package grid with an on-sale calendar.
assertions: Recommends adding package types beyond the fixed full season — at least a mini/choose-your-own package and a flex pass or ticket-credit option
Computes the new-package acquisition target needed to hold flat as base × (1 − renewal rate), using the user's numbers
Distinguishes first-year from multi-year subscriber renewal and recommends a first-year onboarding sequence before increasing acquisition spend
Lays out a cohort renewal pricing ladder (loyalty lock, early-renewal incentive, new-subscriber price, lapsed win-back) and a down-sell to flex/mini before losing a subscriber
Sequences on-sales so renewals close before single tickets go on sale, and presents a package grid (type, shows, price by zone, discount vs. single, benefits, restrictions)
Advises that benchmark rates are sector studies to re-check and that published prices should get knowledgeable staff review before going live

evals.prompt: we're on eventbrite for our 220-seat black box and people keep complaining the $28 ticket turns into like $33 at checkout. should we just eat the fees? also is there any legal issue here? we're in Colorado
evals.expected_output: Explains embedded vs. passed-through fees with checkout math, flags the FTC fees rule's all-in price display requirement and that Colorado has its own all-in pricing law, and notes Eventbrite's fit limits for reserved-seat seasons; tells the user to verify current fees and rules.
assertions: Explains the embedded (absorbed) vs. passed-through fee choice and shows worked math of what the org would net or what face value would need to rise to
States that the FTC's fees rule requires the all-in total price, including mandatory fees, to be shown upfront and that it applies to nonprofits
Notes that Colorado is among the states with its own all-in pricing law and that buyers' state laws can apply
Tells the user to verify current platform fees and the legal rules at the source before publishing a fee schedule
Recommends displaying the all-in price everywhere (ads, site, emails, box office) with fees itemized underneath

evals.prompt: Our second show is selling way below forecast — 38% sold two weeks out. Our ED wants to cut prices on the website by $15 across the board, and also wants to pull the school matinee program into this conversation since teachers keep asking about curriculum guides and teaching-artist visits. What do we do? (Mid-size theater in Maryland, 600 seats.)
evals.expected_output: Advises against visible public price drops in favor of targeted promo codes, notes late-booking patterns mean softness two weeks out may not predict a flop, keeps subscriber rates untouched, handles school-matinee booking logistics, and routes curriculum and teaching-artist work to the arts education skill.
assertions: Advises against a visible public price drop and recommends targeted promo codes for defined groups (e.g., students, educators, lapsed subscribers) instead
Notes that post-pandemic audiences book late, so weak sales two weeks out do not by themselves predict a flop and marketing spend should be held through opening
States that subscriber per-ticket rates must not be affected by price changes

Covers only school-matinee box-office logistics (e.g., flat per-student price, chaperone comp ratio, deposits) and routes curriculum guides and teaching-artist residencies to nonprofit-arts-education-programs
